extracted.intended_audience: judges, patent attorneys, and law students working on U.S. patent-infringement equity remedies
extracted.subtask_description: Rules and principles governing when and how courts of equity (injunctions, accounts) may hear and decide patent-infringement disputes, especially relative to remedies at law and timing (patent expiration, pendency). Focused on U.S. federal practice and precedents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary jurisdiction in courts of law
rubrics_metrics.description: Primary jurisdiction over all suits for infringement resides in courts of law; whenever adequate redress can be obtained by an action on the case for damages, or other common-law proceeding, equity has no jurisdiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equity is a residual forum. If damages or other common-law remedies provide adequate redress, the suit belongs at law and will be dismissed in equity (see §1094(1)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Equity takes jurisdiction when remedy at law is inadequate
rubrics_metrics.description: Where an adequate remedy at law does not exist, whatever the cause or degree of such inadequacy, equity will take cognizance of the action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of inadequacy: need to prevent future infringements; need for discovery; protection of equitable interests; assertion of equitable defenses; or where an account of profits cannot be obtained by methods known to courts of law. In such cases equity may entertain original proceedings and administer entire relief (§1094(2)-(3)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Equity retains jurisdiction until complete redress
rubrics_metrics.description: If equity properly takes jurisdiction, it will retain the cause until complete redress has been afforded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Once equity jurisdiction is legitimately invoked, the court will not dismiss the case merely because the precise equitable remedy (e.g., injunction) later becomes unavailable; it will continue to provide any equitable relief necessary to secure full vindication (§1094(2)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Injunctions for post-expiration use/sale of articles made during patent life
rubrics_metrics.description: An infringing act after patent expiration can only be committed by use or sale of patented articles that were made for that purpose during the life of the patent; in such instances equity has jurisdiction at whatever period the action is brought and may restrain the defendant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equity may enjoin use or sale after expiration where the articles were made during patent life (cases cited §§1092, notes). By contrast, where only past infringement damages exist and can be recovered at law, equity will generally not enjoin after expiration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accounting of profits in equity (scope differs from law)
rubrics_metrics.description: An accounting of profits may be had in equity as incidental to other equitable relief; the items recoverable in 'profits in equity' may be more extensive than those obtainable at law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Profits in equity must nevertheless be limited to gains received and cannot embrace remote pecuniary benefits; but equity may permit recovery of advantages flowing from the defendant's use that would not be recoverable at law. Where an account can be adequately had at law, equity will not entertain the suit for that sole purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of patent expiration on suits begun in equity in good faith
rubrics_metrics.description: A suit commenced in equity in good faith while the patent is in force is not affected by the patent's subsequent expiration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If jurisdiction in equity was properly invoked while the patent was alive, expiration pending suit does not oust equity jurisdiction; the court may still grant relief appropriate to the case (see §1093 and cited cases).

rubrics_metrics.name: Suit filed after patent expiration solely to obtain accounting is evasion
rubrics_metrics.description: A suit commenced without intent to ask for an injunction or other equitable relief, but merely to procure an accounting after the patent has expired (where equity would have no jurisdiction if then brought), is an evasion of the law and will be dismissed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts will dismiss bills that are purely pretexts to obtain accounts after expiration; timing and good faith matter (§1083 notes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Bill filed too late for injunction will be dismissed
rubrics_metrics.description: A bill filed too late to obtain a preliminary injunction before the patent expired (i.e., where adequate relief at law exists) will be dismissed, often with costs to the defendant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases hold such tardy filings are to be dismissed; but if the bill was filed timely as to one of several patents, equity may retain jurisdiction as to the others (§1083 notes, Mershon v. Pease Furnace Co., etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Amendment to add injunction prayer can confer equity jurisdiction if in good faith
rubrics_metrics.description: A bill filed before patent expiration but not originally praying for a preliminary injunction may be amended to insert such a prayer at any time; if done in good faith it may confer equity jurisdiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts have allowed amendments adding an injunction prayer where the amendment is bona fide and thereby properly invokes equitable relief (see Adams v. Bridgewater Iron Co.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Equity will award discovery and ancillary relief even after expiration when necessary
rubrics_metrics.description: Where equitable relief of any form is necessary (e.g., discovery required), equity will have jurisdiction although the patent has expired, and an account or damages may also be awarded as incidental relief.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equity may retain jurisdiction to grant discovery and ancillary remedies after expiration, provided such equitable relief was or could have been legitimately sought (§1092, §1093 notes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Equity will not entertain matters already litigated elsewhere or where party had opportunity
rubrics_metrics.description: Equity will not entertain a matter which a party has had a chance to litigate in another court.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the plaintiff had a prior adequate forum or opportunity, equity may decline jurisdiction; courts require a reasonable prospect of affording ultimate equitable relief (§1094 and notes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Equity jurisdiction cannot be conferred by waiver or agreement of parties
rubrics_metrics.description: A want of jurisdiction in equity, because an adequate remedy exists at law, cannot be waived by acquiescence or agreement of the parties; it is an incurable defect that may be taken advantage of at any stage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts will dismiss suits when lack of equitable jurisdiction is noticed, regardless of party agreements (see §1095 and Spring v. Domestic Sewing Mach. Co.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Local jurisdiction in equity generally identical with at law (personal service required)
rubrics_metrics.description: Actions in equity may be brought in any district within which the defendant can be personally and lawfully served with process; the rule is the same as that in actions at law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Service by attachment of property cannot confer jurisdiction; a defendant served personally in the district may be sued there. Defect of service may be waived by appearance unless timely objected to (§1096 and notes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Equity territorial enforcement limited — suit must be in district where decree can be enforced
rubrics_metrics.description: A decree in equity can be enforced only against the person of the defendant and within the territorial jurisdiction of the court which passed it; if relief cannot be afforded without authority beyond the district, the court must decline jurisdiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequently, prevention of future infringements or other relief enforceable only in a given territory generally requires suit in that district even if legal remedies could be obtained elsewhere (§1097). Exception: district of defendant's residence may enforce decrees against resident defendants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rules for suing corporations and service on officers
rubrics_metrics.description: A corporation can be sued in any district in the State from which its charter was received, or in any foreign district in which it can be served with process according to local law; service upon its officers within the district is not, absent local provisions to the contrary, service on the corporation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appearances by officers do not necessarily waive defects in corporate service; marshals' returns must show personal service within the district when defendant is sued out of his district (§1096 notes and §935 references).

rubrics_metrics.name: All persons affected by decree must be parties; plaintiffs must have legal or equitable interest
rubrics_metrics.description: Parties to a suit in equity comprise all persons (natural or artificial) who can be affected by the decree. Any person having, at the time of infringement, either a legal or an equitable interest in the patented invention and capable of being prejudiced by the infringing act may be a plaintiff.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legal and equitable owners may be joined; if no party plaintiff has a legal or equitable interest, the suit must be dismissed. Local law may determine who has such interests (see §1098 and cited cases).

rubrics_metrics.name: Equitable accounting constrained by scope and remoteness
rubrics_metrics.description: Even when equity awards an account of profits, the accounting must be limited to gains received and cannot encompass remote pecuniary benefits; the difficulty lies in determining items entering 'profits in equity' versus law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because equity's measure of recompense may differ from law, courts must carefully limit recoverable items to those fairly representing the defendant's gains from infringement; examples and cases illustrate divergent measures (§1092 notes).
